verdict: Avoid new fruit and vegetable processing exposure in Nashik for now; lend only to frozen and snack processors with contracted volumes and tight monthly stock reporting, and decline pulp and export-led units.
title: Nashik Fruit & Vegetable Processing: a note to the credit manager
narrative: Collect from customer: peak inventory days, buyer credit terms, and share of revenue from exports. **Pricing power is thin because raw material is the largest cost line and moves with weather** [9]; a processor who cannot pass fruit price through absorbs it in margin.

## What has changed now
**The data call is Avoid at 44, and the news flow is worse, so the call stays Avoid.** India-wide exports are down 9.6% Apr-to-date in USD [D], and the peer set confirms the pain: Foods & Inns Q4 FY26 profit fell 16% on lower volumes, with realisations down 25.3% [4]. **Maharashtra electricity demand grew 6.0% Apr-to-date against India's 9.5%, a local stress signal** [D], even as state GST collections grew 8.6% against India's 6.1% [D]. Locally, unseasonal rains have hit crops around Jalgav and lemon growers are waiting on compensation [2]; that is a raw-material supply and quality risk, not a demand story. **Bank credit is growing 26.3% YoY against output of 5.1%** [D], so the system is lending faster than the real economy is producing; do not add to that gap in this sector.

## Where the growth is
**The one clear positive is the ₹124 crore Prime Fresh project in Nashik, part of the 12 national horticulture clusters launched in October 2026** [3]. That is a capex and anchor-buyer signal, not yet a lending signal. **Pursue frozen and snack processors with domestic quick-service and retail contracts**; the peer's frozen food volume grew about 39% YoY in Q2 FY26 [6] and snacks and pulp are described as showing tremendous growth [7]. **Avoid pulp-only exporters and gherkin units exposed to a single season** [8], and avoid any unit whose sales ledger is dominated by one overseas buyer.

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the season, not the balance sheet.** Size the limit to one harvest cycle, take the stock and receivables of named buyers as primary security, and keep a cash-flow cover covenant. **Take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, buyer-wise sales, and a quarterly drawing-power certificate**; if stock days exceed the agreed cap, ask for the buyer contract and the ageing. **When a proposal lands, check the export share and the realisation trend first; if realisations are falling while volumes rise, ask for the price list and the buyer-wise margin.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for inventory building while sales stay flat, receivables ageing past 90 days, and a shift from domestic to export buyers.** If a unit's electricity consumption falls while its stock rises, ask for the production log. **If the promoter brings in a new lender or the stock statement stops arriving, treat it as a signal to reduce exposure.**

Realisations falling with flat volumes -> ask for price list and margin by buyer
